source.excerpt: Wipe out the imagination. Stop the pulling of the strings. Confine thyself to the present. Understand well what happens either to thee or to another.
trail: Quote sites credit the line to Marcus Aurelius’ Meditations but rarely give a book or section, e.g. Goodreads ↗.
The passage is Meditations 7.29; George Long’s 1862 translation reads “Wipe out the imagination… Confine thyself to the present,” per the Internet Classics Archive ↗.

Other scholarly translations render the same section very differently — the Loeb-style text on Wikisource ↗ has “Define the time which is present,” showing the popular wording is a specific translation choice.
source.excerptNote: George Long’s 1862 translation of Meditations 7.29. The widely shared “Confine yourself to the present” simply updates the archaic “thyself.”

source.rightsNote: The confirmed wording “Confine thyself to the present” comes from George Long’s 1862 English translation of the Meditations, long in the public domain. The Greek original is ancient; the popular “yourself” form is a trivial modernization of Long’s public-domain text rather than a distinct copyrighted rendering.

author.bio: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus (121–180 AD) was Roman emperor from 161 until his death and the last of the “Five Good Emperors.” His private notebook, the Meditations, was written in Greek for his own guidance during military campaigns and never intended for publication. It survives as one of the foundational texts of Stoic philosophy, full of terse reminders to master the mind and live in the present moment.

misattribution.heading: How it circulates
misattribution.intro: The attribution is correct — this really is Marcus Aurelius — but the way the line travels online obscures its source and softens its wording.

items.why: The scholarly translations read “Confine thyself to the present” (George Long, 1862 ↗) or, in the Loeb tradition, “Define the time which is present” (Wikisource ↗). The circulating “yourself” is a modern pronoun update.
Most quote pages, such as Goodreads ↗, name only “Marcus Aurelius” or “Meditations” with no book or section, making the line look like a floating aphorism rather than part of the argument at 7.29.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought and the near-exact wording are authentically Marcus Aurelius, Meditations 7.29 — verified against George Long’s translation ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The Meditations was never a book meant for readers — it was Marcus Aurelius’ private set of reminders to himself, written in Greek while on campaign. Book 7, section 29 is a rapid-fire string of imperatives to discipline the mind: erase distorting mental images, resist the impulses that pull you off course, and “confine thyself to the present.”

The instruction sits at the heart of Stoic practice: the past and future are outside our control and exist only as thoughts, so attention and duty belong to the present moment. Modern “live in the now” culture has adopted the line, which is why the cleaner “Confine yourself to the present” now circulates far more widely than any scholarly translation.
context.detailsSummary: The full run of imperatives in 7.29
detailsBody: In George Long’s translation the section reads: “Wipe out the imagination. Stop the pulling of the strings. Confine thyself to the present. Understand well what happens either to thee or to another. Divide and distribute every object into the causal and the material.” The isolated fifth-word command is only one link in a chain of self-directed instructions.
